intro:
If you have started reading the New Testament with fresh eyes, you have probably noticed something strange. The apostles quote the Old Testament constantly, and they often quote it in ways that do not seem obvious at first. Matthew says a verse about Israel coming out of Egypt is really about Jesus. Paul says a rock in the desert was Christ. Hebrews spends whole chapters on priests and animal sacrifices and then says all of it was pointing somewhere the whole time. A new reader can be forgiven for wondering whether the writers were just grabbing verses that sounded useful and bending them to fit.

The honest answer is that they were doing the opposite. The apostles believed they had met the end of the story in person, and so they went back and read the whole story again in his light. They were not pulling single verses out of context for convenience. They were reading the Old Testament the way you reread the first chapter of a book after you finish it, seeing the early pages full of things you missed the first time. Jesus himself taught them to read this way. On the road to Emmaus he opened the Scriptures and showed two grieving disciples how Moses and all the prophets had been speaking of him.

What follows is a plain guide to the main ways the New Testament handles the Old. None of these methods is a trick. Each is a way of reading the one long account of God and his people as it moves toward a single point. Learn to see these patterns and a lot of what once looked surprising will start to look like careful, faithful reading.

methods.name: Direct promise and fulfillment
methods.definition: Sometimes a prophet plainly predicts something, and the New Testament records it coming true. The promise and the fulfillment line up in a straightforward way.
methods.example: The prophet Micah, writing roughly seven centuries before Jesus, said the ruler of Israel would come out of Bethlehem, a small and unimportant town. When Matthew records the birth of Jesus in Bethlehem, he quotes Micah directly. The chief priests even cite the same verse when Herod asks where the Messiah is to be born. This is the simplest category. A specific prediction, a specific event, and a clear match between them.

methods.name: Typology
methods.definition: A type is an earlier person, event, or institution that God designed as a pattern pointing forward to something greater. The earlier thing is real in its own right, and it is also a shadow of what was coming.
methods.example: Paul calls Adam a pattern of the one who was to come, then sets Adam and Christ side by side. Adam brought sin and death through one act, and Christ brought righteousness and life through one act. Another clear case is the bronze serpent. In the wilderness, dying Israelites were healed when they looked up at a serpent Moses lifted on a pole. In John 3, Jesus says that just as Moses lifted up that serpent, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, so that whoever looks to him in faith will live. The old event was true history, and it was also built to foreshadow the cross.

methods.name: The law fulfilled in Christ
methods.definition: The temple, the priesthood, and the system of animal sacrifices were never the final goal. They taught Israel about holiness and forgiveness, and they reached their meaning and their end in Jesus.
methods.example: The letter to the Hebrews makes this argument at length. The blood of bulls and goats could never truly take away sin, the writer says, so the sacrifices had to be repeated again and again. They were a picture of the real thing. Jesus enters not a tent made by hands but the true sanctuary, and he offers not the blood of animals but himself, once for all. The old system worked the way a road sign works. It pointed somewhere, and once you arrive you no longer need the sign.

methods.name: Israel's story recapitulated in Jesus
methods.definition: Israel was called to be God's faithful son and repeatedly failed. The New Testament shows Jesus reliving the key moments of Israel's life and succeeding exactly where the nation fell.
methods.example: Hosea 11:1 says, out of Egypt I called my son, and in its own setting it looks back on God rescuing the nation of Israel from slavery. Matthew quotes that line about the child Jesus being brought back from Egypt, treating Jesus as the true Son who walks Israel's path. The same pattern appears in the forty days Jesus spends in the wilderness being tested. Israel wandered forty years in the desert and grumbled and failed. Jesus faces the tempter for forty days, answers every temptation with Scripture, and does not break. He is the faithful Israel that Israel never managed to be.

methods.name: Continuity and escalation
methods.definition: A promise first given to Israel is not discarded but expanded and raised to a higher level in Christ and the church. The promise stays the same in kind and grows in scope and depth.
methods.example: Through the prophet Jeremiah, God promised a new covenant, one in which he would write his law on the heart and remember sin no more. Hebrews quotes that whole passage from Jeremiah 31 and announces that Jesus is the one who brings this new covenant into effect. The promise made to a single nation centuries earlier is not shrunk. It is enlarged to reach people from every nation, and it is grounded in a forgiveness that finally holds.

methods.name: Reading the Psalms as pointing to the Messiah
methods.definition: Many of the Psalms were songs and prayers of David and the kings of Israel, and the New Testament reads them as also voicing the experience and reign of the Messiah who would come from David's line.
methods.example: Psalm 22 opens with the cry, my God, my God, why have you forsaken me, and goes on to describe pierced hands and feet and enemies casting lots for the sufferer's clothing. Jesus speaks that opening line from the cross, and the Gospel writers see the rest of the scene unfolding in his crucifixion. Psalm 110 runs the other direction, picturing a king seated at God's right hand who rules over his enemies. Jesus and the apostles quote it more than any other Old Testament passage to describe his exaltation and reign. The same songbook holds both the suffering and the throne.

closingNote: Scholars do genuinely debate how closely each New Testament writer leaned on the original setting of the verses they quote, and faithful readers do not all land in the same place. The church has long held both truths together, reading the Old Testament for what it meant to the people who first received it and for how the whole of it points to Christ.
